meta.title: Who really said "If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Emma Goldman never wrote it. The line is a 1973 T-shirt abridgement of a passage in Living My Life — her biographer Alix Kates Shulman explains how.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Goldman's words. A 1973 T-shirt slogan condensed from Living My Life (1931), p. 56 — the origin story told by her own biographer.

answer.label: Not Emma Goldman’s words — a 1973 T-shirt paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: Goldman never wrote or spoke this sentence. It is an abridgement of the dancing episode in her 1931 autobiography Living My Life, condensed onto T-shirts in early 1973 by the anarchist printer Jack Frager — a story Goldman’s biographer Alix Kates Shulman told firsthand ↗, adding that she searched Goldman’s texts for the statement and “it was nowhere to be found.” The sentiment is genuinely hers; the wording is not.

source.heading: What Goldman actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Volume one, 1931, Alfred A. Knopf, New York

Early 1973, on T-shirts printed by anarchist Jack Frager

source.excerpt: At the dances I was one of the most untiring and gayest. One evening a cousin of Sasha, a young boy, took me aside… he whispered to me that it did not behoove an agitator to dance. Certainly not with such reckless abandon, anyway… I did not believe that a Cause which stood for a beautiful ideal, for anarchism, for release and freedom from conventions and prejudice, should demand the denial of life and joy. I insisted that our Cause could not expect me to become a nun and that the movement should not be turned into a cloister. If it meant that, I did not want it. “I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody’s right to beautiful, radiant things.”
trail: 1931 — Goldman publishes Living My Life (Alfred A. Knopf). The dancing episode — a young comrade telling her “it did not behoove an agitator to dance” — sits on p. 56 of the full text ↗.

Early 1973 — Anarchist printer Jack Frager asks Shulman for a Goldman photo and a slogan for fundraising T-shirts to sell in Central Park at the festival celebrating the end of the Vietnam War. He returns “a succinct abridgement of Emma’s dance story”: “If I can’t dance I don’t want to be in your revolution” ↗.

Afterwards — The slogan spreads onto buttons, posters, banners, bumper stickers and books, mutating “like a child’s game of Telephone.” Shulman’s own purple T-shirt carries the now-standard “part of your revolution” wording ↗.

Today — Wikiquote ↗ prints the p. 56 passage and notes that “this incident was the source of a statement commonly attributed to Goldman that occurs in several variants,” listing five — including this one.
source.excerptNote: Read it closely: the words “revolution” and “if I can’t dance” never appear. The famous one-liner is a compression of this whole scene into a slogan that fits across a chest.

Knopf, so it is treated as in-copyright and reproduced only in the short extract needed to document the misquotation. The famous one-line slogan itself has no published source at all — it was coined for a T-shirt run in 1973 — so no public-domain status can be claimed for it.

author.name: Emma Goldman
author.heading: Emma Goldman
author.bio: Born in Kaunas in 1869 and dead in 1940, Goldman emigrated to the United States and became its most notorious anarchist orator — jailed for telling the hungry to take bread, for lecturing on birth control, and for opposing conscription. She edited Mother Earth, was deported to Russia, and broke publicly with the Bolsheviks over their repression of workers. Her 1931 autobiography Living My Life is the source text behind the dancing slogan, and it argues something sharper than the slogan does: that a movement for freedom has no right to demand “the denial of life and joy.”

copyAttribution: Emma Goldman never wrote "If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution." The line is a 1973 T-shirt abridgement — made by anarchist printer Jack Frager — of the dancing episode on p. 56 of her 1931 autobiography Living My Life; her biographer Alix Kates Shulman documented its origin firsthand. What Goldman actually wrote was: "I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody's right to beautiful, radiant things." — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: How a T-shirt became a quotation
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually well-documented misquote, because the person who set it in motion wrote a confession. The sentiment is Goldman’s. The sentence is not.

items.why: Shulman recounts that when she collected her shirts in early 1973 she found “a succinct abridgement of Emma’s dance story spread boldly across the shirt” — the first version, “If I can’t dance I don’t want to be in your revolution” ↗. She searched Goldman’s texts and could not find it.
“Part of your revolution” is a mutation of Frager’s line rather than his own wording. Shulman describes it as the version on her purple T-shirt, under a picture of Emma in a wide-brimmed hat ↗.
Shulman notes the form “If I can’t dance to it, it’s not my revolution” appearing in a 1983 ‘non-sexist yet traditional’ Passover Haggadah ↗; Wikiquote lists five variants in all.

The underlying argument — that a movement for freedom has no business demanding “the denial of life and joy” — is verbatim Goldman, from Living My Life ↗. Shulman’s own verdict on the slogan: “the sentiment expressed was pure Emma indeed.”

misattribution.truthLine: What Goldman actually wrote, on p. 56 of Living My Life, was longer and better: “I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody’s right to beautiful, radiant things.” ↗

context.heading: Why this one is worth getting right
lead: Goldman’s scene is not really about dancing. It is about a movement policing its own members’ pleasure: a young comrade takes her aside at a strike-fund dance, tells her gravely that her “frivolity would only hurt the Cause,” and she rounds on him. Her answer is a refusal to let radical politics turn into a cloister — a larger claim than the slogan makes.

The slogan, by contrast, was born as merchandise. In early 1973 an old-time anarchist named Jack Frager wanted Emma Goldman T-shirts to sell in Central Park at the festival celebrating the end of the Vietnam War, and asked Shulman — who had recently published a biography and a collection of Goldman’s essays — for a photograph and a line. What came back on the shirts was Frager’s own compression. Shulman, by her account, hadn’t the heart to object over a couple of dozen dozen shirts, and the line escaped.
detailsBody: Shulman has told this story more than once. A version appeared in Women’s Review of Books in December 1991; the Lilith version, “Invention of a Feminist Sound Bite,” ran in the Winter 2001–2002 issue; a fuller telling, “Dances with Feminists,” ran in Fifth Estate #357, Summer 2002.

The slogan has outgrown its subject: the Amsterdam-based arts organisation If I Can’t Dance, I Don’t Want To Be Part Of Your Revolution ↗ takes its name from the line while openly acknowledging that Goldman never literally spoke it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Alix Kates Shulman states that in early 1973 anarchist printer Jack Frager put an abridgement of Goldman's dance story on T-shirts — the first version reading 'If I can't dance I don't want to be in your revolution' — and that she searched Goldman's texts for the statement and it was nowhere to be found. The page also notes a different version of the piece was published in Women's Review of Books, December 1991, and that this article appeared in the Winter 2001-2002 issue.

Shulman writes that Goldman 'wrote none of the above' versions; that her purple T-shirt carries 'If I can't dance I don't want to be part of your revolution' under a picture of Emma in a wide-brimmed hat; that 'If I can't dance to it, it's not my revolution' appears in a 1983 'non-sexist yet traditional' Passover Haggadah; and quotes the Living My Life passage with a p. 56 citation. It also names the Central Park festival celebrating the end of the Vietnam War as the occasion for the T-shirts.

Wikiquote lists the dancing passage under Living My Life (1931) at p. 56 and appends the note 'This incident was the source of a statement commonly attributed to Goldman that occurs in several variants', listing five variants including 'If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution.'

The full text of Living My Life contains the dancing episode verbatim, including 'it did not behoove an agitator to dance', 'should demand the denial of life and joy', and 'I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody's right to beautiful, radiant things.'
Living My Life was published by Alfred A. Knopf, Inc. (volume one, 1931), in two volumes.

The arts organisation If I Can't Dance states that it has been claimed Emma Goldman never literally spoke the famous words, and that in 1973 a printer rephrased the Living My Life passage into 'If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution.'
Emma Goldman's dates are June 27, 1869 to May 14, 1940; she was born in Kaunas, Lithuania, then within the Russian Empire, and was an anarchist political activist and writer.
